classification.difficultyReason: Translate the one-root condition into an equation in k, reject a candidate that removes the quadratic term, and establish that the discriminant in part (d) stays positive for every admissible k.

content.prompt: Find the values of $k$ for which the following quadratic equations have exactly one real root.

answer.worked:
The equation is quadratic for $k\ne0$. For exactly one real root, set $\Delta=0$.
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-6)^2-4(k)(k)\\\Delta&=36-4k^2\\0&=36-4k^2\\k^2&=9\\k&=\pm3\end{align*}$$
Both values keep the equation quadratic.

For exactly one real root, set $\Delta=0$.
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=[-(k+4)]^2-4(1)(9)\\0&=(k+4)^2-36\\(k+4)^2&=36\\k+4&=\pm6\\k&=-10\text{ or }2\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$k=\frac43$.

Set $\Delta=0$ and check that the equation still has a root at each candidate value.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-3k)^2-4(k)(3)\\\Delta&=9k^2-12k\\0&=3k(3k-4)\\k&=0\text{ or }\tfrac43\end{align*}$$
At $k=0$, the equation becomes $3=0$ and has no solution. At $k=\frac43$, the equation is quadratic and $\Delta=0$, so it has exactly one real root.

answer.short:
No value of $k$ gives a quadratic with exactly one real root.

Its discriminant is strictly positive.
answer.worked:
For $k\ne0$, the equation is quadratic.
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=[2(k-2)]^2-4(2k)(-3)\\\Delta&=4(k-2)^2+24k\\\Delta&=4(k^2+2k+4)\\\Delta&=4(k+1)^2+12\end{align*}$$
Since $\Delta\ge12$, it cannot equal zero. There is no value of $k$ that gives a quadratic with exactly one real root.
